reads.best: Deterministic, configurable signals can nudge Hermes out of retry loops without adding a network service or blocking tool calls.
reads.worst: The packet only directs the model to delegate; the plugin does not enforce that escalation, and its sole unit-test file offers limited assurance for the many lifecycle hooks.

reads.best: Case-aware hooks check quotations against registered documents before supported writes and keep citation findings and deadline confidence visible, with extensive regression fixtures.
reads.worst: The native plugin falls back from Hermes secrets to a CourtListener token stored in a separate file, violating catalog rule 11; quotation guards also deliberately pass uncheckable content.

reads.best: It adds a practical extraction and crawl path with page/depth/deadline bounds, per-target URL policy checks, and tested failure handling.
reads.worst: It requires a separate reachable Crawl4AI server, and does not itself search the web or provide extraction without that service.

reads.best: Serious engineering: tiers, protected objects, parameter binding, audit log, offline and live test suites, Desktop dashboard.
reads.worst: Audience is niche (AD admins), and the password for WinRM needs an env passthrough for cron.

reads.best: Combines searchable art, deterministic scene composition, layout diagnostics and a Desktop pane with hash-verified, bounded downloads.
reads.worst: The README and PR explicitly disclose that the Desktop pane has not been proven on a live Hermes Desktop host.

reads.best: The code validates legal moves, guards against stale asynchronous replies, and tests a deadline fallback so a stalled model cannot make a second late move. (Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/itsflownium/gambit-hackathon/9c725ad0b04c2bc32f16efd00dfc1b4d421360cb/README.md)
reads.worst: It needs a separately installed Stockfish and a working model for conversational coaching, and the documented verified catalog scope is macOS only. (Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/itsflownium/gambit-hackathon/9c725ad0b04c2bc32f16efd00dfc1b4d421360cb/README.md)

reads.best: It changes ongoing Hermes context with persistent local memory and includes tool and hook tests for the core memory flow.
reads.worst: The implementation's custom resonance scheme is not meaningfully validated for retrieval quality, and the README is diluted by extensive unrelated material.

reads.best: Background job followers and native chat/Desktop delivery add real integration, and the pin gates ad spending and publishing on human approval.
reads.worst: It requires a paid external Glorya service, whose creative generation and campaign execution cannot be inspected in this pinned repository.

reads.best: A real context-engine extension preserves recent tool-call structure and includes tested pruning and deterministic digest fallbacks.
reads.worst: Fresh installs have no wired pin-capture path, and optional router sizing reads an API key directly from config.yaml instead of Hermes’s secret scope.

reads.best: Real skeletal motion playback, mood envelopes, avatar uploads and lifecycle integration go well beyond a decorative prompt.
reads.worst: The authenticated PSFN bridge validates only the initial loopback URL and uses default redirect-following urllib, leaving a potential bearer-token leak through a redirected endpoint.

reads.best: Lifecycle hooks, group-scoped boards, bounded stored excerpts, and stale-update guards provide useful local coordination without automatic nudges.
reads.worst: Question and promise classification is heuristic, CLI/TUI chats are untracked, and reload recovery depends on a private state.db schema.

reads.best: Changes how Hermes delegates (a backend plus outcome learning), stdlib only, fails closed with no routes, has unit and e2e tests.
reads.worst: Needs hand-written routes config; benefit is hard to see for most users and the heuristics are keyword-based.

reads.best: Meaningful-result hooks and verified source quotations give users portable continuity across Hermes and other agents.
reads.worst: Calendar, weather, usage and job features depend on the separate Kokpit database, and quote presence alone does not prove a proposed next step is justified.

reads.best: Adds a whole new messaging platform with careful fail-closed handling and scoped secrets.
reads.worst: Needs an external daemon and hand-copying the adapter into Hermes, and uses private host functions.

reads.best: Candid README, about 72 tests across Python, vitest and Playwright, reproducible bundle with readable source in the repo, and screenshots.
reads.worst: Locked to Hermes 0.22.6 because it reads private PTY_REGISTRY internals; the PR is still open with the maintainer's change request not addressed; no Desktop plugin.

reads.best: A substantial bilingual session-management UI is backed by extensive routing, filesystem-safety and completion-state regression tests.
reads.worst: Live owner-routing acceptance remains incomplete, and the IDEA.md endpoint echoes supplied project ownership rather than independently authenticating it.

reads.best: A real native memory provider that changes what Hermes remembers, with layers, hook mapping and a mirror of builtin memory.
reads.worst: Keyword-only FTS recall, auto-capture with little filtering, daemon threads, and the README lists only a store unit test.

reads.best: It extends Hermes delegation through the public provider API and tests exact pins, refusal categories, lack of fallback, and configuration immutability.
reads.worst: It cannot verify that an endpoint is local or authenticate caller-declared prior outcomes, and installation documentation still uses repository placeholders.

reads.best: The concurrent adversarial/architect/performance perspectives make model deliberation an actual Hermes tool rather than a prompt convention.
reads.worst: The pinned snapshot has only a small validation test surface for a networked multi-model system, plus optional Telegram code and a simulated offline path that make operational behavior less convincing.

reads.best: A real hook-to-proof workflow includes replay and tamper guards, preserved evidence on failure, selective disclosure, examples and a Desktop surface.
reads.worst: Proofs cover an agent-authored ledger and configurable policy units rather than complete activity or real spend; single-party setup limits trust, and unconditional fcntl imports break the advertised Windows path.

reads.best: Dual-target backup and actual restore drills address the valuable problem of preserving a user’s agent state.
reads.worst: Secrets.load falls back to a password file even without a standalone-mode guard, contrary to catalog rule 11; restore confirmation is only an agent-supplied boolean.

reads.best: Clever zero-token cron design with a deterministic, well-tested alert engine (25 offline tests, CI), host allowlist, timeouts and no keys or trading.
reads.worst: Modest scope, and the watchlist claimed to be shared safely across chat, CLI and cron is guarded only by a threading lock, so separate processes can lose updates.

reads.best: Small, deterministic and honest: 600 lines, 32 tests, no network or model calls, and a limits section that says exactly what it cannot catch.
reads.worst: The detector is text counting on a guessed test-file pattern, blocks legitimate test deletion, and the README admits it was not yet tested on Linux, macOS or Docker.

reads.best: A fail-closed enforcement hook with about 87 tests (188 cases with parametrization), CI, an allowlisted child environment and process-group timeouts.
reads.worst: Does nothing without the separately installed Open-Ready CLI, only guards the terminal tool, and claims to read the origin remote, which no code does.

reads.best: Bounded stripped-environment probes, conservative provenance reports and tripwire tests address a concrete source of local-agent failures.
reads.worst: It does not measure the terminal tool's final PATH, and the POSIX login-shell implementation leaves Windows unsupported.

reads.best: Observes Hermes's own API traffic with no network or credentials, saved atomically.
reads.worst: Claims more than the code: it is passive, not proactive; the rolling window is never used; and the refresh tool duplicates the status tool.

reads.best: Original idea with tests that prove later chapters are never read.
reads.worst: Niche use, no UI, and the model's own knowledge of famous books can still spoil.

reads.best: An allowlist interlock, hardware-free mock porch and local HTTP tests make the camera workflow inspectable without uploading frames.
reads.worst: Authenticated cameras take passwords embedded in settings URLs and pass RTSP URLs to ffmpeg argv instead of using Hermes secret scope, conflicting with catalog credential rules.

reads.best: Persistent per-chat league with a cron referee that settles from real results, plus a written escrow program.
reads.worst: Commits a devnet deployer keypair in escrow/devnet/deployer.json and has a referee key sign escrow settlements of staked money without a per-payment human approval.

reads.best: Over 100 tests and careful evidence handling with budgets and expiry.
reads.worst: Its own README calls it a local pilot, not a released catalog plugin, and the task is one a search-plus-prompt skill largely covers.

reads.best: Strictly read-only (DB opened read-only, no --apply), clean code, and 29 test cases that check it writes nothing.
reads.worst: overlap() requires every cron field to overlap, ignoring cron's day-of-month OR day-of-week rule, so some collisions can be wrong; it has no UI, and a stray CLAUDE.md holds the developer's personal notes.

reads.best: It uses live SDK usage state and honestly limits recent-session history to metadata instead of inventing historical token totals.
reads.worst: No tests are shipped, fallback prices are a small hardcoded table, and the status-chip cost tooltip does not distinguish estimates from reported cost ([Code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Whydiriki700/token-dashboard/39949565742a74d00ec03c9921c7ef3eee208d88/desktop/plugin.js)).

reads.best: Network-free, path-scoped engine with 35 test files and JSON schemas.
reads.worst: Much of the bundled data/schemas is in Spanish and the README miscounts its own tools (18 vs 19); niche audience.

reads.best: The pane connects installer checks, local node RPC, diagnostics and read-only agent tools, with tests for offline states and wallet operations.
reads.worst: The advanced export reads wallet keys from disk and returns a decrypted private key to the pane rather than using Hermes secret storage; the installer hash is displayed, not checked against an expected hash.

reads.best: Balanced real-item controls, deterministic sampling, ground-truth tests, and fail-fast provider handling make the narrow benchmark auditable. (Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/salch-cred/bluff/4c43c96be7a4411d91ebc0b7de59086639ce0507/judge.py; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/salch-cred/bluff/4c43c96be7a4411d91ebc0b7de59086639ce0507/README.md)
reads.worst: Scoring trusts the explicit exists field rather than checking whether the answer text fabricates details, so this is a narrow lower-bound probe rather than a general hallucination measure. (Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/salch-cred/bluff/4c43c96be7a4411d91ebc0b7de59086639ce0507/judge.py)

reads.best: Closes a learning loop safely: it only writes candidates for review and never live skills.
reads.worst: Only useful to Puppetmaster users; one hook, no tests in the plugin folder.

reads.best: Holds no keys: trades come back as unsigned transactions for the user's own wallet, and the drand draw commits to a future round so the proof can be rechecked.
reads.worst: No tests at all, and six of eight tools serve one vendor's prediction-market product that few Hermes users will touch.

reads.best: Charming, well-tested Desktop/dashboard novelty with original art.
reads.worst: A joke with no practical use for most users.

reads.best: Careful token handling: Hermes's server_json discovery attaches the token, the server is marked untrusted, and model pulls need authorization.
reads.worst: No executable code at all; every tool lives in a closed app needing macOS 26.2+ on Apple silicon, and the only test is a manifest validation.

reads.best: Its tools compute full-file statistics and use a SQLite authorizer to reject query writes.
reads.worst: Only one local integration test covers the main path; loading large files and building the in-memory SQL table have no resource budget.

reads.best: Uses an untrusted server declaration, Hermes-managed OAuth setup, and a clear distinction between manufacturing-rule checks and actual circuit correctness.
reads.worst: The bundled server declaration cannot authenticate on its own; users must add OAuth manually, and no checker implementation or tests are included at the pin.

reads.best: It offers a concrete enrichment service with OAuth managed by Hermes and repeatedly calls out that paid operations consume account credits.
reads.worst: The pinned package is primarily instructional skills and remote connection metadata; the actual MCP implementation is hosted, and end-to-end OAuth and paid workflows were not tested.

reads.best: Pure-stdlib deterministic checker with clear disclosure; arithmetic done in code, not by the model.
reads.worst: Very niche CSV format, no tests and no Hermes-specific integration.

reads.best: The server source includes streaming export parsing, freshness and truncation reporting, privacy modes and meaningful parser and profile-boundary tests.
reads.worst: The actual plugin launches an npm release rather than the pinned repository code, needs a first-run download and manual health exports, and adds no deeper Hermes lifecycle integration.

reads.best: Well-engineered helper (fixed endpoint, no redirects or proxy, size limits, clear errors) with offline tests in CI and an unusually candid privacy and affiliate disclosure.
reads.worst: It is a niche shopping connector to a vendor's hosted service, so the plugin adds no Hermes-specific capability.

reads.best: It uses a core lifecycle hook to make session-level usage and cost visible instead of relying on provider dashboards.
reads.worst: The pinned repository has no tests and a small implementation, while its pricing table and token shapes can become stale or incomplete.

reads.best: Per-client SQLite billing, opt-in activity capture and authenticated live updates make a usable local freelancer dashboard.
reads.worst: _newest_mtime does not exclude the current .pow-time directory, so its own database writes can be mistaken for client work and distort automatic billing.

reads.best: Addresses a broadly useful need (visual QA / PDF generation / scraping JS-heavy pages) with clear documentation.
reads.worst: No tests anywhere in the repo, and almost all real logic lives off-repo in the paid third-party SaaS, leaving little the plugin itself does beyond a thin API-key pass-through.

reads.best: Deterministic template normalization and streaming file iteration can reduce large repetitive logs to compact counts without network services or dependencies.
reads.worst: Bounded-memory claims overreach: complete lines are read before truncation and timeline buckets are capped only after accumulation, while regex matching has no timeout and no automated tests ship.

reads.best: Honest disclosure of what it sends where; read-only apart from suggest_bot, with no key needed.
reads.worst: It ships no code, the server's source is not published, and it helps you find bots for a different product (Grok) rather than improving Hermes; its own skill already covers this with plain curl.

reads.best: Four focused read-only tools use Hermes secret lookup and bounded HTTP and git calls without extra dependencies.
reads.worst: No tests ship, multi-project discovery silently chooses the first project, and invalid arguments or subprocess failures can escape despite the README's never-raise claim.

reads.best: A small readable package documents Hermes OAuth setup, untrusted write approvals and workspace selection without handling credentials itself.
reads.worst: The pinned submission contains no server implementation; tool behavior changes remotely, access requires a Pro workspace, and the PR reports no live Hermes OAuth/tool-call verification.

reads.best: Tidy multi-client packaging with a consistency check script, the server marked untrusted, and skills that tell the agent never to ask for or print a token.
reads.worst: No code of its own, needs an Inboxapp team with API v2 (private rollout, 404 otherwise), and sending or deleting is left to the remote server and skill wording.

reads.best: Deterministic offline scans and bounded receipts provide a small, readable auditing tool with tests for common credential formats.
reads.worst: The advertised fail-closed gate only returns a BLOCK label; its post-tool hook logs after execution and neither prevents outbound sends nor changes results.

reads.best: The package declares an untrusted server and the skill asks the user to confirm message recipients and contents. [PR and pinned-package review](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/151331)
reads.worst: The required OAuth setup creates an overriding server entry without the untrusted flag, dropping enforced approval for send and scheduling tools, as the catalog review identifies. [PR and pinned-package review](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pull/151331)

reads.best: Local template editing, field previews, clipboard export, and illustrated setup make the small writing workflow approachable.
reads.worst: The agent-side feature only injects fixed style text, and the repository contains no tests for the Desktop template and brief workflows.

reads.best: Careful privacy-minimal logging (O_NOFOLLOW, 0600, no args stored).
reads.worst: No README and no tests in the plugin folder; ~140 lines with narrow value.

reads.best: Ambitious vision with docs, a dashboard and HF token from the secret store.
reads.worst: Specialist outputs are mostly hard-coded canned strings (e.g. a fixed SQL query) despite claims of a live network, so it claims more than the code does.

reads.best: Ambitious local training and runner integration with many tools.
reads.worst: Opaque, hard-to-read code with large unverifiable claims, a self_modify tool and a sprawling scripts tree; no clear user.

reads.best: URL access fails closed without Hermes SSRF protection and note writes use atomic replacement.
reads.worst: No tests are shipped, concurrent note updates can overwrite each other, and the response-size check happens after the HTTP client has buffered the body.

reads.best: The envelope validator rejects nested credential material and the result verifier distinguishes a proposed call from completed work, with focused offline tests.
reads.worst: Despite the orchestration branding, tools return templates and flags without dispatching work, persisting decisions or creating agents, so a skill covers most of the value.
